meta.title: Who really said "Most Conversations Are Simply Monologues Delivered in the Presence of a Witness"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Mark Twain. Margaret Millar wrote it in her 1942 mystery novel The Weak-Eyed Bat, page 117 — and she wrote "a witness," singular.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Most Conversations Are Simply Monologues Delivered in the Presence of a Witness'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Mark Twain. It is Margaret Millar, in her 1942 novel The Weak-Eyed Bat — verified to page 117 by Quote Investigator.

answer.label: Not Mark Twain — actually Margaret Millar
answer.sourceLine: The line is a piece of dialogue from The Weak-Eyed Bat, the 1942 mystery novel by Margaret Millar — Quote Investigator traced it to page 117 and verified it against library scans ↗. Millar wrote “a witness,” singular; there is no substantive evidence that Mark Twain ever wrote or spoke it.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 1942 — published for the Crime Club by Doubleday, Doran & Co., Garden City, New York
Page 117, verified against library scans by Quote Investigator

source.excerpt:
“As a matter of fact, have you never noticed that most conversations are simply monologues delivered in the presence of a witness?”
“No,” Jakes said.
trail: 1942 — Margaret Millar publishes The Weak-Eyed Bat, her second Paul Prye mystery, for the Crime Club at Doubleday, Doran & Co.; the sentence appears on page 117. Quote Investigator, verified with scans ↗
1990 — Robert Byrne’s fourth Best Things Anybody Ever Said reprints the saying, still credited to Millar, but with the plural “witnesses.” See the 1990 citation in the chronology ↗
2013 — the business book Real Influence hands the line to Mark Twain; this is the earliest Twain ascription Quote Investigator documents. Documented by Quote Investigator ↗
Today — reference sources that check their attributions still put it under Millar’s name. Wikiquote’s Monologue page ↗
source.excerptNote: The line is dialogue, not authorial narration — it is put to a character named Jakes, who is unimpressed. Quote Investigator obtained scans of the 1942 edition through the library system of the University of North Carolina at Greensboro.

author.name: Margaret Millar
author.heading: Who was Margaret Millar?
author.bio: Margaret Millar was born in Kitchener, Ontario in 1915 and died in Santa Barbara, California in 1994. She married Kenneth Millar — later famous as Ross Macdonald — in 1938, and out-published him for a stretch: her early novels featured the poetry-quoting psychiatric detective Paul Prye, of whom The Weak-Eyed Bat (1942) was the second outing. She won the Edgar Award for Best Novel in 1956 for Beast in View and was named a Grand Master by the Mystery Writers of America in 1983.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on, and why
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook famous-name upgrade: a working mystery novelist writes a good line, an anthology reprints it, the wording softens, and eventually the biggest name in American humour absorbs it.

items.why: Quote Investigator states plainly that there is no substantive evidence Twain wrote or spoke the statement, and documents the Twain ascription only from 2013, in the business book Real Influence by Mark Goulston and John B. Ullmen — where it appears as “Most conversations are monologues in the presence of witnesses.” Twain’s own documented remark on the subject, in a letter of 20 August 1886 to Clara Spalding, runs quite differently: all conversations, he wrote, are but debates. See the chronology ↗

Byrne’s fourth Best Things Anybody Ever Said compilation credited Millar correctly but printed the plural “witnesses,” departing from the 1942 text. The plural is the form that later circulated under Twain’s name. Quote Investigator flags the change ↗

A 1987 management book quoted the popular speaker Leo Buscaglia on conversations being “alternating monologues” — a related thought, but not this sentence, and not a route to Millar’s wording. Cited in the same investigation ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Margaret Millar wrote it, in The Weak-Eyed Bat in 1942, on page 117, with “a witness” in the singular — verified against library scans by Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why the line drifted to Twain
lead: Millar’s sentence is a joke told in a book, by a character trying to be clever — and it works because it is faintly insulting to everyone in earshot. That is exactly the register people associate with Mark Twain, which is most of the explanation for how a 1942 Canadian mystery novel lost its byline.

The mechanism is visible in the paper trail. Quote Investigator shows the saying travelling correctly credited through a quotation anthology, picking up a small wording change along the way, and then, seven decades after the novel, in print under Twain’s name in a 2013 management title — and once a line is there, it is effectively laundered.
context.detailsSummary: The older ideas behind the line
detailsBody: The observation was not new in 1942, and Quote Investigator lays out the lineage: an 1863 Richmond newspaper serial joked about a conversation that was “more properly speaking, the two monologues”; a 1901 essay said Hamlet’s conversations were monologues; and a 1918 book recorded an English traveller complaining that Americans do not converse but indulge instead in “a series of monologues.”

Closest of all, Rebecca West opened a story in her 1935 collection The Harsh Voice with the observation that conversation is an illusion — there are only intersecting monologues. Millar’s contribution is the sharp final image, the witness, rather than the underlying idea.
context.pull: Millar wrote “a witness.” The version pinned on Twain says “witnesses.”

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes there is no substantive evidence Mark Twain wrote or spoke the line, credits it to Margaret Millar's 1942 novel The Weak-Eyed Bat at page 117 (verified with scans via UNC Greensboro), notes Millar's original singular 'witness', records Robert Byrne's 1990 collection printing the plural 'witnesses', the 1987 Leo Buscaglia 'alternating monologues' attribution, Twain's 20 August 1886 letter to Clara Spalding ('All conversations are but debates'), the 1863/1901/1918 precursors, the 1935 Rebecca West passage, and the 2013 attribution to Twain in Real Influence by Mark Goulston and John B. Ullmen.
Wikiquote's Monologue page lists 'Most conversations are simply monologues delivered in the presence of a witness.' under Margaret Millar's name.

Margaret Millar was born 5 February 1915 in Berlin (now Kitchener), Ontario and died 26 March 1994 in Santa Barbara, California; she married Kenneth Millar (Ross Macdonald) in 1938; she won the Edgar Award for Best Novel in 1956 for Beast in View and the MWA Grand Master Award in 1983; The Weak-Eyed Bat (1942) was the second Paul Prye novel.

The Library of America Women Crime Writers site confirms Millar's dates and Canadian origin, the psychiatric detective Paul Prye first appearing in The Invisible Worm (1941) and later in The Weak-Eyed Bat and The Devil Loves Me (both 1942), the Edgar for Beast in View, and the 1983 MWA Grand Master title.

Syndicate Books announced in October 2014 that it had acquired North American publishing rights to the complete works of Margaret Millar - all 27 books - from her estate, negotiated with Craig Tenney at Harold Ober Associates, with print volumes and ebooks published in 2015.

The Online Archive of California finding aid for the Margaret Millar papers states that literary rights are retained by the creators of the records and their heirs, and directs requests to publish or reproduce copyrighted material in excess of fair use to the Margaret Millar Charitable Remainder Unitrust.
The Internet Archive holds 'Collected Millar: The First Detectives' (Syndicate Books, New York, 2017), whose contents include The Weak-Eyed Bat; the item is access/lending restricted.

The Center for Mark Twain Studies runs an 'Apocryphal Twain' series and states that there is perhaps no greater testament to Twain's lasting reputation than the habitual misattribution of miscellaneous wit and wisdom to his name.
